items.title: Show HN: Cerea – yet another self-hosted LLM chat front end
items.summary: Here is Cerea, a self-hostable, open-source (Apache 2.0) chat+agent frontend for LLMs. It works alone with any OpenAI-compatible inference provider, but it's way better when coupled with the model gateway I'm also developing, Pystino ( https://github.com/paoloviviani/Pystino ). I came to this after struggling to find a hosted chat interface that was truly open source, that I really enjoyed to use, and that was simple enough to be shared and used by family. In particular, I was looking for something that could provide the smooth and integrated user experience of commercial products for the tasks needed by family (e.g., document editing, form filling, notes and knowledge management), but backed by open models hosted wherever I decide. Then it became richer, now supporting: remote coding agents (wrapping Opencode), delegation and coordination between agents, integration between chat/projects and code agents (this one to me is a pain point for Claude, which I use at work), projects, RAG, rich artifacts support, schedules, and more. You can try it yourself, either cloning the full repo and head to Cerea/kit, or just the deploy kit with a script ( https://github.com/paoloviviani/Cerea#quick-start ). It's just a docker compose with a ./configure script that helps to generate a sensible .env for the specific scenario. It works in the browser and as a PWA on mobile. I hope you'll enjoy, feel free to reach out for questions.

items.title: Show HN: Thinker – Trim context and cache knowledge to extend agent usage limits
items.summary: I’ve been doing a lot of solo development lately and found myself hitting Claude token limits halfway through the week constantly. Even with a Max plan, I’d have to switch over to Codex or Cursor, and it would be a bit difficult to get used to the nuances of each harness. It’s still a problem for me, but I finally built Thinker to save me some tokens and help me get a bit more out of my coding agent subscriptions. I started off a bit in the dark about how token billing works, and had to dig deeper to figure out what workflows ended up hurting my budget the most. By far, it was large context windows. Claude tries to help out on costs by offering prompt caching - which is sort of a bandage on the bigger problem: context bloat. I find that my context window gets bloated with unneeded tokens in two main ways: Tool outputs from subtasks that are long finished. File reads, Bash commands, MCP outputs, etc. Main idea is that the model finished the work but carries the weight of it for every subsequent call - translating to wasted token usage. CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md getting way too big. Lots of content gets dumped into these files as your agents work in your repo. I found that it’s not clear what is actually useful to be included there. Every token here counts, because it will be paid for in every session, and its cost scales linearly with the duration of your session. Thinker addresses both of these issues. We have a proxy that wires in between your harness and model to cut out old context that we determine is no longer needed for your current task. Based on the provider you’re using, we determine the right time to batch enough context to cut that justifies the cache re-write cost, which gets paid off after X subsequent calls. We also analyze your sessions and figure out which parts of your instruction files don’t really get used - and send you suggestions to cut or compress those sections. Thinker will kick off a subagent to do that work for you and open a PR you can review. Finally, we use your sessions to record knowledge notes by distilling your sessions with a cheap model (Haiku, Luna). These notes are then served at prompt time via a cross-encoder, also on your machine, that decides whether a note is relevant to the user’s prompt. Here are some data points to show how exactly Thinker saves you coding agent costs: https://thinker.sh/see-the-data If you’re hitting problems at all with usage limits, it’d be great to hear how you’ve been trying to mitigate it. Our open-source repo here (MIT License): https://github.com/yoavshmariahu/thinker

items.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
items.summary: Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet ( https://rivet.dev ) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3. Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle. It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable. Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. This led us to extend our game server orchestrator to support what we call Rivet Actors today: many lightweight workers with in-memory state and durable storage. By using actors, we were able to serve tens of millions of monthly active users. As agents grew in popularity, it became clear that running agents in sandboxes is inefficient. Sandboxes are expensive, mostly idle, and slow to start. Developers started using actors because they are far more memory efficient (72 KB baseline for actors vs 512 MB for a minimal sandbox) and fast to start (4.9 ms p99 for actors vs 1.7 s p99 for sandboxes). For example, Amp is using Rivet to orchestrate multiplayer agents. They originally tried to build on Cloudflare Durable Objects, but couldn’t launch because of the platform’s limitations and unresponsive support. They migrated to Rivet Actors in a weekend and deploy on-prem. Rivet’s flexible architecture lets them adapt it to their own use cases without being constrained by a framework or the memory, storage, and runtime limits of Cloudflare Durable Objects. Under the hood, Rivet is backed by S3 while maintaining SSD speeds. Why S3? Previously, Rivet ran on FoundationDB. However, we were surprised to find that companies are storing orders of magnitude more data on Rivet Actors than in Postgres, such as large session transcripts, agent artifacts, and full POSIX filesystems. As their data grew, they had to start paying for SSDs that sat mostly idle with old transcripts. This led us to double down on S3 as our primary storage medium without sacrificing performance. This choice means that data stored on Rivet is 10× cheaper than on EBS gp3 while maintaining SSD speeds. It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost: When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors. This architecture lets Rivet provide 1.07 ms durable writes (3 AZ, p99), 1.36 ms reads (p99), and 138 ms reads from object storage (p99). We’ve spent a lot of time making sure that Rivet can run wherever you need it. Self-hosting requires deploying a single Rust binary with S3 as the only dependency, Rivet Cloud lets you deploy dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region, and BYOC lets us deploy Rivet to your VPC without having to operate it yourself. Rivet also runs identically in local dev as in production, since Rivet is a lightweight binary that runs anywhere Rivet Actors can be written in TypeScript or Rust. Out of the box, they support agents (Pi Durable), workflows, real-time, multiplayer, running AI-generated code, Durable Streams, and integrations with tools like Vercel’s Eve and Turso. See all of our available guides, or point your agent at them: https://rivet.dev/docs/#guides Try it out now, by reading our quickstart guides ( https://rivet.dev/docs/ ) or ask your agent: “Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then build a multiplayer chat agent and run it locally.” We’d love to get feedback on your experience with Rivet! We’re deeply invested in making Rivet an easy-to-self-host, flexible, and efficient way to run agentic workloads. GitHub: https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet Architecture: https://rivet.dev/docs/architecture/ Benchmarks: https://rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking/ Self-hosting: https://rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/

items.title: Show HN: Resource Manager – Manage all resources on the computer
items.summary: Hello everyone, I'm BIOcanse. Windows Task Manager has inaccurate readings and limited monitoring items. Various hardware adjustments are also very separated—CPU, GPU, and fans all require their own individual software. Their interfaces and interactions are primitive, and they often overwrite each other's configurations. Moreover, driver management of the CPU and GPU is too clumsy, and the memory usage issue on Windows is also very serious. So I made Resource Manager to view and manage all these resources in one place, making monitoring and scheduling work seamlessly together. Monitoring: This software integrates almost every possible monitoring item, letting you look at your computer from a God's-eye view! Scheduling: One of the core features. It uses algorithms I wrote to optimize memory usage and reasonably schedule processes across multiple CPU cores. It also supports GPU scheduling, which means it can switch the GPU a program uses while it is running. For example, after launching a game, if GPU usage is high or VRAM is about to overflow, it will move the remaining software to another GPU (for most personal computers, this is usually the integrated GPU). Reporting: Many times, computer performance problems are actually just caused by a single program or driver—the benefits of 100 programs optimizing themselves cannot make up for a memory leak in just one program. The reporting page reports abnormal resource usage (CPU, GPU, memory, VRAM, disk read/write, network traffic, and causing system interruptions). Hardware Adjustment: All the parameters you can think of for hardware like the CPU and GPU can be adjusted here. However, my own setup is an AMD CPU + NVIDIA GPU, so other setups still need to be verified. I do have several computers with Intel CPUs to verify Intel CPU support, but I really do not have a single AMD GPU. Although most of it uses mature open-source dependencies, there may still be risks, so please use it with caution.

items.title: Show HN: Revline – An open-source AI-native video editor
items.summary: Hi HN, I'm Zura, and I'm building Revline, a fully agentic video editor. Revline can take your rough draft of a short or long video, watch it, understand the content, and make edits like a real editor would. It's been super useful for me (not biased, obviously). I want to post more content, but my output has never matched how frequently I want to post. Editing takes too much time, and every video I don't finish is waste of time(and money). The problem I've had (and still have) with current "AI video editors" is that they're either single-purpose, closed, or simply don't work well enough. If I still have to manually interfere with the timeline when using something advertised as an AI video editor, how much editing is the AI actually doing? For the same reason, I don't want to use three different platforms for clipping, editing, and creating launch videos. I think those should be features of a single video editor, not separate products. I like to describe Revline as a general-purpose AI video editor. It isn't limited to rough drafts or turning long videos into short clips. You can also create motion-design launch videos. I specifically did not included hand-customizations ( like customizing VFX, transition, or even subtitle colors ), because once again, if you have to still hand-edit while using platform to reduce friction of editing, you might aswell save money not using it. AI can already learn your styles, taste, remember throughout editing, that's the repeatable part every creator/non creator has to do while creating content frequently. Under the hood Revline loads agent with 100+ tools to edit video, i have defined set of lanes (Which anthropic calls "Progressive disclosure", but i call it "lanes") to load specific set of skills and tools only needed for specific edit you are working with, so each type of edit gets it's own "harness". Footage is analyzed using Deepgram, Gemini agentic-mode, or handing specific frames to agent directly ( depends on situation ), while motion graphics are generated as React/GSAP components ( hyperframes used as previewing and exporting engine). Rendering runs through FFmpeg and distributed workers. The same editing tools are also exposed over MCP, so Claude Code, Codex, and other agents can edit projects directly. The entire editor is open-source under Apache 2.0. PRs, contributions, and feedback are welcome! My ultimate goal is to build a video editing experience that existing platforms simply can't offer. I'd love to hear what HN thinks, especially where you think an agent-first approach to video editing might fall short. Website: https://tryrevline.com GitHub: https://github.com/revlinehq/Revline

Show HN: Penthera, offline pentest security scanner (open-source, rule-based)
items.summary: local non-AI security for your app/site! For years I had a long .txt file with hundreds of manual security checks I ran before pushing a (client) app/site to live; I am really a rookie compared to the real cyber experts, but just covering the basics has saved us many times from malicious attacks on our infrastructure. With the sprawl of AI generated vibecoded apps (I love it, i think creating should be accessible, but so should be cyber safety) and AI coding tools, our code goes to LLM providers but we'd never know what exactly happens behind the scene, hype harness is just rules imo. As i've started my phd and not building apps (anymore for a living;) I'd decided to open source my rule-based system with some easy onboarding; use it through CLI, NPM, MCP, skill/agent (whatever they might call it in a few years). Its super helpful as a free, open-source alternative to run these checks in your codebase. Having a non-AI solution that costs $0 tokens might not outperform a SOTA security model of a big company; but running internal blue/red hat pentests 24/7/365 should be the norm for a safer internet; having it open-source making it a whitebox system and I hope many people contribute their lists. Its not bulletproof but we score #1 on some public benchmarks among free tools (npm malware, PyPI malware and JS injection bugs) so thats encouraging you can run it pre-commit hook, CI etc - working on a "watch" function that runs it live. Have some flags like --deep for a very intense pentest (SQLi, SSTI, SSRF, XSS, command injection) so be careful and only your own URLs. Also --ai opts-in a local Ollama (or if you want paid also fine) model to find things beyond my rules (the LLM never decides on findings).
